landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.name: Sainte-Chapelle
landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.teaser: Louis IX's chapel of 1248, where fifteen-metre windows leave almost no wall at all
landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.story: Louis IX built this chapel inside his palace to hold relics he had bought, chief among them the Crown of Thorns, and saw it consecrated on 26 April 1248, well under a decade after work began. You enter through the low, painted lower chapel, then climb a tight spiral stair into the upper one, and the stone more or less disappears: windows some 15 metres tall, roughly 1,113 scenes from Genesis to the Passion, red and blue light falling on the floor. The chapel still stands inside the walls of the working law courts, which is why the queue starts at a security gate.
landmarks:Sainte-Chapelle.why: Go on a bright morning and stay in the upper chapel long enough for your eyes to read one window from the bottom up.
facts: Boulevard du Palais, 1er (Île de la Cité), through the law-courts security gate
Daily from 09:00; to 19:00 Apr-Sep and 17:00 Oct-Mar (seen Jul 2026)

landmarks:Palais Garnier.name: Palais Garnier
landmarks:Palais Garnier.teaser: Marble stairs, gilt foyers, a Chagall ceiling, and the water tank under the stage that fed a novel
landmarks:Palais Garnier.story: Charles Garnier won the competition for a new opera house as a little-known architect in his thirties, and the building opened in 1875: onyx, coloured marble and gold on a staircase built for watching people arrive. The Grand Foyer runs the length of the facade like a palace gallery. Over the red-and-gold auditorium, Marc Chagall's ceiling of 1964 sits in bright patches of colour around the great chandelier. Under the stage lies a tank of groundwater the builders could not drain; Gaston Leroux put it into The Phantom of the Opera in 1910, and the legend has outgrown the book.
landmarks:Palais Garnier.why: Better still than the daytime visit: book a ballet night and see the staircase doing the job it was built for.

landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.name: Bourse de Commerce
landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.teaser: The old grain exchange of Les Halles, with Tadao Ando's concrete drum set inside its dome
landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.story: This round hall at the edge of Les Halles began in the 18th century as the city's grain market, later got its iron-and-glass dome and became the commodities exchange, and in 2021 reopened as François Pinault's museum of contemporary art. Tadao Ando's answer to the old building was to leave it alone and stand a smooth concrete cylinder, nine metres high, inside the rotunda; a walkway on top brings you face to face with the 19th-century painted frieze of world trade running round under the dome. The galleries ring the drum on three floors, filled with rotating shows from Pinault's collection.
landmarks:Bourse de Commerce — Pinault C.why: Climb to the top of Ando's cylinder for the frieze at eye level, then look straight down into the drum.

art:Musee Rodin.name: Musée Rodin
art:Musee Rodin.teaser: The Thinker among clipped box, 2,000 rose bushes, and the gilt dome of Les Invalides over the wall
art:Musee Rodin.story: The Hôtel Biron was built in 1727-1732 to designs by Jean Aubert, and by 1908 its rooms were let cheaply to artists; Rodin took studios here, later the whole house, and it opened as his museum on 4 August 1919. Indoors: The Kiss in marble, the plaster studies, a room for Camille Claudel. Outside, about three hectares: some 2,000 rose bushes of about a hundred varieties around the house, gravel walks, and the bronzes in open air. The Thinker sits on his tall plinth among the box trees; at the far end stands The Gates of Hell.
art:Musee Rodin.why: Buy the garden-only ticket on a fine afternoon and give it two hours; it is the cheapest great sculpture show in Paris.
facts: Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00, closed Mondays, 1 Jan, 1 May and 25 Dec; closing times differ between listings, and the garden shuts earlier in winter (Oct 2026, check)

art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.name: Musée de la Vie Romantique
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.teaser: Ary Scheffer's 1830 house down a cobbled lane, reopened in February 2026, tea in the greenhouse
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.story: In 1830 the Dutch-born painter Ary Scheffer moved into this green-shuttered house at the end of a cobbled lane off rue Chaptal, and his Friday evenings drew the whole Nouvelle Athènes quarter: Chopin, Delacroix, Pauline Viardot and George Sand, who lived a few minutes away. Sand never lived here, but her furniture, jewellery and a plaster cast of her arm are kept on the ground floor, Scheffer's own paintings upstairs. The house closed in September 2024 for restoration and reopened on 14 February 2026 with its displays rearranged. Behind it, roses, clematis and bellflowers grow around a small glass conservatory.
art:Musee de la Vie Romantique.why: Have tea and a scone in the greenhouse garden; the permanent collection is free, so you can do both in an hour.
facts: Free for the permanent collection; temporary exhibitions charged (Oct 2026)

art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.name: Musée de Montmartre
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.teaser: The oldest house on the hill, where Renoir painted The Swing in the garden you sit in
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.story: The house at 12 rue Cortot goes back to the 17th century and is the oldest on the Butte. In 1875-1876 Renoir rented rooms here and worked in the garden behind: The Swing was painted there, and the Bal du Moulin de la Galette a few streets away in the same months. Later the building held Suzanne Valadon and her son Maurice Utrillo, and her studio has been reconstructed upstairs, stove, easel and all. The collection tells the cabaret years through posters and objects: Toulouse-Lautrec, the Chat Noir's shadow theatre. Three terraced gardens step down the slope toward the vines (the Clos Montmartre has its own card).
art:Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir.why: Climb to Valadon's studio, then take a coffee on the terrace in the gardens where Renoir worked.

culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.name: Musée Nissim de Camondo
culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.teaser: A banker's Petit Trianon on Parc Monceau and a family story that ends at Auschwitz; shut for works
culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.story: Count Moïse de Camondo, of a Sephardic banking family from Constantinople, had René Sergent build this house in 1911-1914 on the lines of Versailles' Petit Trianon, with a garden by Achille Duchêne opening onto Parc Monceau, to hold his 18th-century panelling, furniture, Sèvres porcelain and silver. His son Nissim, a pilot, was killed in aerial combat in 1917; Moïse named the house for him and left it to the nation, opening as a museum in 1936. In the war his daughter Béatrice, her former husband and their two children were deported and murdered at Auschwitz, and the family ended. The house has been closed since 4 August 2024.
culture:Musée Nissim de Camondo.why: Hold it for a return trip; for now, Jacquemart-André (its own card) is the open collector's house nearby.
facts: 63 rue de Monceau, 8e, on the edge of Parc Monceau

culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.name: Musée Jacquemart-André
culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.teaser: A banker's mansion on boulevard Haussmann, full of Italian painting, with tea under a Tiepolo ceiling
culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.story: Édouard André, banker and collector, met the society painter Nélie Jacquemart when she painted his portrait; years later they married, and every spring they travelled to Italy and came back with crates. The result fills the house he had built on boulevard Haussmann: Botticelli, Uccello, Mantegna, Tiepolo frescoes, alongside French 18th-century rooms and a double staircase curling up from the winter garden. Nélie left it all to the Institut de France. After a EUR 6.5 million restoration it reopened on 6 September 2024. The old dining room is now the café, Le Nélie, and its ceiling is a real Tiepolo.
culture:Musée Jacquemart-André.why: Book the café for lunch or tea and eat under the Tiepolo ceiling; the Italian rooms upstairs come after.

culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.name: Musée Gustave Moreau
culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.teaser: A Symbolist's house hung frame to frame, up an iron spiral stair, exactly as he planned it
culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.story: Late in life Gustave Moreau decided that his house in the 9th should become a museum of his own work, and he had the upper floors rebuilt as two great top-lit studios joined by a wrought-iron spiral staircase. He died in 1898; the museum opened in 1903 and has barely changed. Some 1,300 paintings, watercolours and drawings are here, the canvases hung edge to edge from floor to ceiling, and hundreds more drawings sit in hinged wooden cabinets you swing open yourself. Downstairs, the small private flat he kept for his parents' furniture and memories is a quiet contrast to the jewelled Salomés above.
culture:Musée Gustave Moreau.why: Open the pivoting drawing cabinets in the studios; most visitors walk past them.
facts: Wednesday to Monday 10:00-18:00, closed Tuesdays (Oct 2026); it closed during the summer 2026 heatwaves

culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.name: Galerie Vivienne & Passage des Panoramas
culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.teaser: Mosaic floors at Vivienne, engravers' and stamp dealers' windows at the Panoramas, ten minutes apart
culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.story: The Passage des Panoramas was cut through around 1799-1800 by the American James Thayer, between two rotundas showing painted panoramas, and in 1817 it was among the first places in Paris lit by gas. Today it is narrow and close: stamp and postcard dealers, small bistros, and the carved shopfront of the engraver Stern, who arrived in 1834. Galerie Vivienne, built from 1823 and opened in 1826, is the grand one: mosaic floors, half-moon windows, a long glass roof, an antiquarian bookshop and old shop signs. Of the dozens of passages once in Paris, about twenty survive (the passages curiosity has the longer story).
culture:Galerie Vivienne & Passage des P.why: Walk Vivienne first for the floors, then cross to the Panoramas and on over the boulevard into Passage Jouffroy, all under glass.
facts: Galerie Vivienne between rue des Petits-Champs and rue Vivienne; Passage des Panoramas from 11 boulevard Montmartre to rue Saint-Marc, 2e

culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.name: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.teaser: A Mansart mansion in the Marais, where a boar peers from a cabinet and owls line a ceiling
culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.story: The museum fills the 17th-century Hôtel de Guénégaud, the only private house by François Mansart still standing, and the Hôtel de Mongelas next door, and is run by the foundation of François Sommer, hunter, industrialist and conservationist. It is staged rather than catalogued: a ceiling feathered with owls, a boar's head looking out of a cabinet, a fox curled on a chair, old guns and hunting paintings hung beside contemporary artists invited to answer them. The subject is the long, uneasy bargain between people and animals, and it is handled with wit. The panelled rooms are rarely crowded.
culture:Musée de la Chasse et de la Natu.why: Come on Wednesday evening, when it stays open late and the Marais rooms are close to empty.
facts: Tuesday to Sunday 11:00-18:00, Wednesdays to 21:30 except July-August; closed Mondays and public holidays (Oct 2026, listings)

art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.name: Grande Mosquée de Paris
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.teaser: Mint tea poured from a height under fig trees, in a mosque courtyard that turns 100 this year
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.story: The Grande Mosquée was built in 1922-1926 in Hispano-Moorish style and inaugurated in 1926, raised as a tribute to the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War; 2026 is its centenary. It is a working place of worship, and the café maure on its outer side is open to anyone with no ticket: a tiled patio with blue-and-white zellige, a fountain, fig trees, sparrows waiting under the tables. Waiters pour sweet mint tea from high above small glasses and bring trays of gazelle horns and honey pastries. Inside the mosque, a guided visit shows the garden courtyard and the minaret.
art:Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden.why: Take the tea on the patio after the Jardin des Plantes across the street; visit the mosque itself any day but Friday.

craft:Do this one.name: École Lesage
craft:Do this one.teaser: Two hours with a hook and needle at the school of Lesage, the embroiderer behind Paris haute couture
craft:Do this one.story: Lesage has embroidered for the Paris couture houses since 1924, and joined Chanel's craft houses in 2002; its atelier now works at le19M, the Chanel-built home for some 700 artisans on the north-east edge of the city. Hubert Barrère has been its artistic director since 1 December 2011, the day François Lesage died. The house opened its school in 1992, and alongside professional courses it runs evening sessions for beginners: once a month, 18:00 to 20:00, at most twelve people, theory then practice, and you take home a small embroidered sample. Your teacher is one of the school's embroiderers; Barrère runs the atelier, not the class.
craft:Do this one.why: It is the one Paris couture trade you can sit down and practise, inside the house that still does it for the runway.
facts: Embroider a small sample by needle, with a short introduction to the couture techniques

craft:Other one.name: Paris-Ateliers gilding course
craft:Other one.teaser: Five days learning to lay gold leaf on old wood, in the City of Paris's own craft classes
craft:Other one.story: Paris-Ateliers is the City of Paris's programme of art and craft classes for adults, and its short courses have included a five-day introduction to gilding with gold leaf, taught by the gilder Claire Bartoli. You bring a small old gilded object of your own, a frame or a mirror, and work through the slow preparation that comes before the leaf goes on: the layers, the sanding, the bole. Groups are of eight. The 2024 edition ran 19-23 February at EUR 380. Missing: no 2026 session was published when this was checked, so treat it as a lead to follow, not a booking.
craft:Other one.why: Bring your own battered frame; the course is built around restoring a real object, not a practice board.

craft:Other two.name: La Cuisine Paris
craft:Other two.teaser: Three hours of croissant, pain au chocolat and pain aux raisins, taught in English by the Seine
craft:Other two.story: The Paris croissant is a laminating craft: butter folded into dough, rolled and folded again until the layers bake apart into flakes. La Cuisine Paris, a cooking school on the quai de l'Hôtel de Ville facing the Île Saint-Louis, teaches it in a three-hour hands-on class that also covers pain au chocolat and the snail-shaped pain aux raisins, with places limited and dates through 2026. It is clear, well run and in English. Missing: this is a school kitchen, not a working bakery, and no named baker of standing teaches the class; you learn the method, not a house's own.
craft:Other two.why: The closest thing to laminating dough in Paris that a visitor can book on a fixed date.
facts: Make croissants, pains au chocolat and pains aux raisins from laminated dough

craft:What is sold as Paris craft.name: What is sold as Paris craft
craft:What is sold as Paris craft.teaser: The miniature Eiffel Towers on a ring of wire under the tower are made in China and sold illegally
craft:What is sold as Paris craft.story: The men with rings of little gold Eiffel Towers at the foot of the tower and on the Trocadéro are street sellers working without a licence, and their stock comes in by the tonne from China. In 2018 Paris police broke a network bringing the miniatures from China through Aubervilliers, seizing about 20 tonnes and arresting nine people, three of them Chinese wholesalers; the objects did not meet European safety standards. An earlier seizure in July 2013 took 60 tonnes. The city's municipal police in the 7th run regular sweeps to clear the hidden stashes. Nothing about the trinket is a Paris craft.
craft:What is sold as Paris craft.why: Spend the same money on something made by hand in the city: a couture embroidery evening, or a piece from a working atelier.
facts: Any miniature tower bought from a street seller under the Eiffel Tower or at the Trocadéro is imported, unlicensed stock
